Consider an electrolyte \(\mathrm{A_xB_y}\) that dissociates in aqueous solution as

\(\mathrm{A_xB_y} \rightleftharpoons x\,\mathrm{A^{y\oplus}} + y\,\mathrm{B^{z\ominus}}\)

Suppose 1 mole of the electrolyte is dissolved and \(\alpha\) is its degree of dissociation.

Initially : 1 mol of \(\mathrm{A_xB_y}\), 0 mol of each ion.

At equilibrium : \(\alpha\) mol has dissociated, so \((1-\alpha)\) mol of \(\mathrm{A_xB_y}\) remains undissociated, and the moles of cations and anions produced are \(x\alpha\) and \(y\alpha\) respectively.

Total moles of particles after dissociation

\(= (1 - \alpha) + x\alpha + y\alpha = 1 + \alpha(x + y - 1) = 1 + \alpha(n - 1)\)

where \(n = x + y\) is the number of moles of ions obtained from one mole of the electrolyte.

The van't Hoff factor is defined as

\(i = \dfrac{\text{actual moles of particles in solution after dissociation}}{\text{moles of formula units dissolved in solution}} = \dfrac{1 + \alpha(n-1)}{1}\)

Hence

\(i = 1 + \alpha(n - 1)\) or \(\alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1}\)

This is the required relationship. It gives \(i = 1\) for an undissociated solute \((\alpha = 0)\) and \(i = n\) for complete dissociation \((\alpha = 1)\); for a binary electrolyte \(n = 2\) and the relation simplifies to \(\alpha = i - 1\).

How the solubility of a solid changes with temperature depends on the ENTHALPY OF SOLUTION, and is predicted by Le Chatelier's principle applied to the saturated-solution equilibrium.

i. Endothermic dissolution (heat absorbed). Adding heat places a stress on the equilibrium, which is relieved by the endothermic process, so more solute dissolves and the solubility INCREASES with rising temperature. Examples given in the chapter: KCl, and from Fig. 2.1 the solubilities of \(\mathrm{KNO_3}\), \(\mathrm{NaNO_3}\) and KBr increase appreciably with temperature.

ii. Exothermic dissolution (heat released). Here raising the temperature favours the reverse, endothermic direction, so the solubility DECREASES. Examples given: \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Li_2SO_4 \cdot H_2O}\) dissolve in water releasing heat, and from Fig. 2.1 the solubility of \(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4}\) decreases as the temperature is raised.

iii. Some solids are almost unaffected — the solubilities of NaBr, NaCl and KCl change only slightly with temperature (Fig. 2.1).

The chapter adds an important caution: there is NO direct correlation between solubility and exothermicity or endothermicity. The dissolution of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\) is exothermic and that of \(\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}\) endothermic, yet the solubility of both increases with temperature.

(For gases the trend is the opposite: dissolved gas molecules are condensed into the liquid, which is an exothermic process, so the solubility of a gas in water usually decreases as the temperature is raised.)

The freezing point depression of a dilute solution is directly proportional to the molality of the solution:

\(\Delta T_f \propto m\) or \(\Delta T_f = K_f m\)

where \(\Delta T_f = T_f^0 - T_f\) and \(K_f\) is the freezing point depression constant (cryoscopic constant) of the solvent.

Suppose the solution is prepared by dissolving \(\mathrm{W_2}\) g of a nonvolatile nonelectrolyte of molar mass \(M_2\) in \(\mathrm{W_1}\) g of solvent. Then

moles of solute \(= \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2}\), mass of solvent \(= \dfrac{\mathrm{W_1}}{1000}\ \mathrm{kg}\)

so the molality is

\(m = \dfrac{\mathrm{W_2}/M_2}{\mathrm{W_1}/1000} = \dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Substituting this into \(\Delta T_f = K_f m\) gives

\(\Delta T_f = K_f\dfrac{1000\,\mathrm{W_2}}{M_2\mathrm{W_1}}\)

and rearranging for the molar mass,

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_f\mathrm{W_2}}{\Delta T_f\,\mathrm{W_1}}\)

This is the required relationship. Knowing \(K_f\) for the solvent and measuring \(\Delta T_f\) for a solution of known \(\mathrm{W_2}\) and \(\mathrm{W_1}\), the molar mass of the solute is obtained.

A liquid boils at the temperature at which its vapour pressure equals the applied pressure, which for an open vessel is 1 atm = 760 mm.

The diagram (Fig. 2.6 of the chapter) plots vapour pressure against temperature for the pure solvent and for the solution. Two curves are drawn:

- AB, the vapour pressure–temperature curve of the PURE SOLVENT,
- CD, the corresponding curve of the SOLUTION.

At every temperature the vapour pressure of the solution is lower than that of the pure solvent, because a nonvolatile solute occupies part of the surface and fewer solvent molecules escape from it. Hence the curve CD lies entirely BELOW AB. The vertical gap between the two curves widens as the temperature rises, since \(\Delta P = x_2P_1^0\) and \(P_1^0\) itself grows rapidly with temperature.

A horizontal line is drawn at 760 mm. It cuts the solvent curve AB at the temperature \(T_b^0\), the boiling point of the pure solvent, and cuts the solution curve CD further to the RIGHT, at \(T_b\), the boiling point of the solution. Because CD is the lower curve, it needs a higher temperature to climb to 760 mm.

Therefore \(T_b > T_b^0\), and the horizontal separation of the two intersections is the boiling point elevation

\(\Delta T_b = T_b - T_b^0\)

So the boiling point elevation is a direct geometric consequence of vapour pressure lowering: the more the solute lowers the vapour pressure, the further right the solution's curve meets the 760 mm line, and the larger \(\Delta T_b\) becomes. Quantitatively \(\Delta T_b = K_bm\).

The concentration of dissolved \(\mathrm{O_2}\) required is 3.8 mg per litre. Converting to a molar concentration, with the molar mass of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) equal to 32 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(S = \dfrac{3.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g\ L^{-1}}}{32\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 1.1875 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\)

The Henry's law constant follows from the data given, since at 1 atm partial pressure the solubility is \(2.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}\):

\(\mathrm{K_H} = \dfrac{S}{P} = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}{1\ \mathrm{atm}} = 2.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ atm^{-1}}\)

By Henry's law \(S = \mathrm{K_H}P\), so the partial pressure needed is

\(P = \dfrac{S}{\mathrm{K_H}} = \dfrac{1.1875 \times 10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}}}{2.2 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ atm^{-1}}} = 0.054\ \mathrm{atm}\)

A partial pressure of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) of at least 0.054 atm above the water is therefore needed for the fish to survive.

[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints (16.17 mm Hg). Raoult's law gives \(P_1 = P_1^0x_1 = 17 \times 2.7778/(2.7778 + 0.04667) = 16.72\) mm Hg for 2.8 g of urea (60 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)) in 50 g of water, and the dilute-solution approximation gives 16.71 mm Hg — the same to three significant figures. The printed value would require about 8.6 g of urea, and appears to be 16.71 with its last two digits transposed.]

Urea is a nonvolatile, nonionizing solute, so Raoult's law gives the vapour pressure of the solution as \(P_1 = P_1^0x_1\), where \(x_1\) is the mole fraction of water.

Moles of urea (molar mass 60 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)):

\(n_2 = \dfrac{2.8\ \mathrm{g}}{60\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.04667\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Moles of water (molar mass 18 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)):

\(n_1 = \dfrac{50\ \mathrm{g}}{18\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 2.7778\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Mole fraction of water:

\(x_1 = \dfrac{n_1}{n_1 + n_2} = \dfrac{2.7778}{2.7778 + 0.04667} = \dfrac{2.7778}{2.8244} = 0.98349\)

Hence

\(P_1 = P_1^0x_1 = 17\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 0.98349 = 16.72\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

The vapour pressure of the solution is 16.72 mm Hg, a lowering of 0.28 mm Hg. (Using the dilute-solution approximation \(\Delta P/P_1^0 = n_2/n_1\) instead gives 16.71 mm Hg, the same value to three significant figures.)

Both solutes are nonelectrolytes, so \(\Delta T_f = K_fm\) and, for the same solvent, \(\Delta T_f\) is proportional to the molality alone.

A 5% solution by mass contains 5 g of solute in 95 g of water, that is 0.095 kg of water.

Cane sugar, \(M = 342\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(m_{\text{sugar}} = \dfrac{5/342}{0.095} = 0.15389\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

Glucose, \(M = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(m_{\text{glucose}} = \dfrac{5/180}{0.095} = 0.29240\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

For the sugar solution, taking the freezing point of pure water as 273.15 K,

\(\Delta T_f(\text{sugar}) = 273.15\ \mathrm{K} - 271\ \mathrm{K} = 2.15\ \mathrm{K}\)

Since \(\Delta T_f \propto m\),

\(\Delta T_f(\text{glucose}) = 2.15\ \mathrm{K} \times \dfrac{0.29240}{0.15389} = 2.15 \times \dfrac{342}{180} = 4.085\ \mathrm{K}\)

(The ratio of the molalities is simply the inverse ratio of the molar masses, \(342/180 = 1.9\), because the two solutions contain equal masses of solute in equal masses of water.)

Therefore the freezing point of the 5% glucose solution is

\(T_f = 273.15\ \mathrm{K} - 4.085\ \mathrm{K} = 269.06\ \mathrm{K}\)

Citric acid is treated here as a nonelectrolyte solute in acetic acid, so the boiling point elevation obeys

\(\Delta T_b = K_b m\)

Rearranging for the molality,

\(m = \dfrac{\Delta T_b}{K_b} = \dfrac{1.76\ \mathrm{K}}{3.07\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.573\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

The molality of the solution is 0.573 m.

(The mass of acetic acid, 50 g, and the formula of citric acid are not needed for the molality itself. They would be needed only to go further and find the mass of citric acid dissolved: \(0.573 \times 0.050 = 0.0287\) mol, which at 192 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\) is about 5.5 g.)

Two measurements are given, and each supplies one concentration of the same solution — the osmotic pressure gives its MOLARITY, the freezing point its MOLALITY. Combining them with the density gives the molar mass.

From the osmotic pressure, with \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(R = 0.0821\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(M = \dfrac{\pi}{RT} = \dfrac{12.16\ \mathrm{atm}}{0.0821 \times 298.15} = 0.4968\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\)

So one litre of solution contains 0.4968 mol of solute.

From the freezing point, with \(K_f = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\):

\(m = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{K_f} = \dfrac{1.03\ \mathrm{K}}{1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.5538\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\)

The mass of WATER in that litre therefore follows from the definition of molality:

\(\mathrm{W_1} = \dfrac{0.4968\ \mathrm{mol}}{0.5538\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}} = 0.8971\ \mathrm{kg} = 897.1\ \mathrm{g}\)

One litre of solution weighs \(1000\ \mathrm{mL} \times 1.063\ \mathrm{g\ mL^{-1}} = 1063\ \mathrm{g}\), so the mass of solute in it is

\(\mathrm{W_2} = 1063\ \mathrm{g} - 897.1\ \mathrm{g} = 165.9\ \mathrm{g}\)

Hence the molar mass is

\(M_2 = \dfrac{165.9\ \mathrm{g}}{0.4968\ \mathrm{mol}} = 334\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

(The result is sensitive to rounding, because \(\mathrm{W_2}\) is a small difference between two large masses: taking \(R = 0.08205\) and \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\) instead returns 332 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\). Carry the intermediate values to four figures.)

Take 100 g of the mixture, which then contains 30 g of toluene and 70 g of benzene.

Molar masses: toluene \(\mathrm{C_7H_8}\) = 92 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\), benzene \(\mathrm{C_6H_6}\) = 78 \(\mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\).

\(n_{\text{toluene}} = \dfrac{30}{92} = 0.3261\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(n_{\text{benzene}} = \dfrac{70}{78} = 0.8974\ \mathrm{mol}\)

Total moles \(= 1.2235\), so the mole fractions are

\(x_{\text{toluene}} = \dfrac{0.3261}{1.2235} = 0.2665\), \(x_{\text{benzene}} = 1 - 0.2665 = 0.7335\)

The two liquids form an ideal solution, so Raoult's law applies to each component:

\(P_{\text{toluene}} = P^0_{\text{toluene}}\,x_{\text{toluene}} = 36.7\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 0.2665 = 9.78\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

\(P_{\text{benzene}} = P^0_{\text{benzene}}\,x_{\text{benzene}} = 118.2\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg} \times 0.7335 = 86.70\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

By Dalton's law the total pressure above the solution is the sum of the partial pressures:

\(P = 9.78 + 86.70 = 96.5\ \mathrm{mm\ Hg}\)

So the partial pressure of benzene is 86.7 mm Hg, that of toluene is 9.78 mm Hg, and the total vapour pressure above the solution at \(30^\circ\mathrm{C}\) is 96.5 mm Hg.

Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte, \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3COO^{\ominus}} + \mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\), so it gives \(n = 2\) ions per formula unit and is dissociated to the degree \(\alpha = 1.35\% = 0.0135\).

van't Hoff factor:

\(i = 1 + \alpha(n - 1) = 1 + 0.0135 = 1.0135\)

Freezing point, with \(K_f\) for water = 1.86 \(\mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(m = 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}}\):

\(\Delta T_f = iK_fm = 1.0135 \times 1.86 \times 0.1 = 0.1885\ \mathrm{K}\)

Since the freezing point of pure water is \(0^\circ\mathrm{C}\), the solution freezes at

\(T_f = 0 - 0.1885 = -0.189^\circ\mathrm{C}\)

Osmotic pressure at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C} = 298\ \mathrm{K}\), taking molarity equal to molality as the question directs:

\(\pi = iMRT = 1.0135 \times 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}} \times 0.08205\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K} = 2.48\ \mathrm{atm}\)

The solution freezes at \(-0.189^\circ\mathrm{C}\) and its osmotic pressure is 2.48 atm.

The van't Hoff factor is the ratio of the observed freezing point depression to the value expected for a nonelectrolyte of the same concentration.

Observed: \(\Delta T_f = 0^\circ\mathrm{C} - (-0.510^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 0.510\ \mathrm{K}\)

Expected for a nonelectrolyte: \((\Delta T_f)_0 = K_fm = 1.86\ \mathrm{K\ kg\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.15\ \mathrm{mol\ kg^{-1}} = 0.279\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(i = \dfrac{0.510\ \mathrm{K}}{0.279\ \mathrm{K}} = 1.83\)

(The value is below the ideal 2 for \(\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K^{\oplus}} + \mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), because at this concentration some of the ions are held together as ion pairs.)

The volume of the solution is taken equal to that of the water, so 1 kg of water makes 1 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) of solution and the molarity equals the molality, \(M = 0.15\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\). At \(0^\circ\mathrm{C} = 273\ \mathrm{K}\),

\(\pi = iMRT = 1.83 \times 0.15\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}} \times 0.08205\ \mathrm{dm^3\ atm\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 273\ \mathrm{K}\)

\(\pi = 6.15\ \mathrm{atm}\)
